channel.title: The Git Reporter
channel.description: A code-native newspaper of meaningful software change.

item.title: Cline gives a finished agent answer a diff receipt
item.description: Cline’s restored “View Changes” control makes a completed agent turn point to a checkpointed file delta—not just its own verdict.

item.title: API Discovery: Pydantic AI routes Cortex work through Snowflake
item.description: Pydantic AI now has a Snowflake Cortex provider, but a useful trial starts by checking the selected model’s capability boundary—not by assuming one adapter makes every model equivalent.

item.title: CrewAI teaches telemetry to separate the agent from the room
item.description: CrewAI’s agent-assisted telemetry change makes one reusable move: record who drove a process separately from where the process ran.

item.title: Hermes now stops agents from quietly rewriting their own instructions
item.description: A new Hermes Agent write gate treats project instruction files as a persistence surface: even an auto-approved agent must ask a human before it changes the text that can steer tomorrow’s work.

item.title: OpenWork learns to wait for a turn that has actually started
item.description: OpenWork’s new headless-thread client turns a subtle race into an explicit contract: an agent turn is not finished just because its status looks idle.

item.title: A Denied Agent Answer Should Not Survive in Memory
item.description: Microsoft’s experimental Agent Hooks adapter treats a rejected response as a session-history problem too: the verdict is meant to arrive before the reader sees it and before the affected context becomes durable.

item.title: Permissions now travel with Codex’s work environment
item.description: Codex is moving a permission choice out of the thread’s background and into the selected environment that runs the command, applies the patch, sees the image, and carries work to another agent.

item.title: Mastra gives recurring agent reminders a way to disappear
item.description: Mastra’s new transient-signal path lets a processor keep a live instruction near the model without quietly turning that instruction into remembered conversation—and its public commit shows coding agents in the work.

item.title: Tau Will Ask Before It Reads a Project’s AGENTS.md
item.description: Tau’s new Project Trust layer turns local instructions, skills, prompts, themes, and extension candidates into a directory-specific decision before they become ambient agent input.

item.title: A Local HTTP Callback Can Stop Qwen Code’s Next Tool Call
item.description: Qwen Code’s opt-in Tool Guard gives managed ACP deployments a small local API that can allow or deny a supported top-level tool call at its final execution boundary.

item.title: The Agent Can Refile a Worktree, Not Rewrite the Filing Cabinet
item.description: Kilo Code’s new Agent Manager move gives an agent a way to reorganize parallel work—only through a live inventory, a targeted command, and a hard boundary around the recovery file.

item.title: Agent Behavior wants to make good conduct a versioned artifact
item.description: Braintrust and Basis propose a tiny BEHAVIOR.md standard as the answer key between runtime instructions and agent evals. The file is easy; writing conduct that remains observable across real trajectories is the actual work.

item.title: A green check is not proof an agent ran
item.description: Pydantic AI turned several ways a coding-agent workflow can silently do nothing into tested policy checks. The transferable craft is to test the execution graph, not just the agent prompt.

item.title: An Approval Cannot Outlive the Conversation That Asked for It
item.description: Cline fixed a small but revealing failure in its VS Code extension: change a message while a command approval is waiting, and the old run could keep waiting forever—then catch answers meant for the new one.

item.title: QM is trying to turn the personal agent into company infrastructure
item.description: Y Combinator's new open-source harness does not win its case by running Codex or Claude in Slack. Its more consequential bet is that every person and room needs a clearly owned memory, workspace, permission set, schedule, and durable computer.

item.title: CrewAI: role-based multi-agent orchestration after the demo
item.description: CrewAI's current source makes a useful correction to the role-playing pitch: a multi-agent crew becomes an operable system only where it carries state, records its progress, and proves what happens after a stop.

item.title: Browser Use: the control boundary between an agent and the live web
item.description: Browser Use’s latest harness release and its own session examples make a harder point than a benchmark: browser automation only becomes legible when profile, destination, and data authority are named controls.

item.title: The Supervision Derby finish: which coding-agent repo made control more real?
item.description: The finish is a split decision: Codex makes filesystem policy travel into capability discovery; Qwen Code makes a fork’s tool gate survive resume; OpenHands and Gemini CLI make narrower but useful controls reachable.

item.title: OpenHands: separating the software agent from the sandbox it works in
item.description: A new healthy-local-backend fallback makes the project’s larger argument concrete: the thing that helps a person steer an agent must stay legible even when the agent is running somewhere else.

item.title: API Discovery: Make the Model Own Its Web Search
item.description: Mastra’s new webSearchTool is deliberately not a generic search client: it selects a provider-native tool from the active model or fails where the provider boundary is unclear.

item.title: Builder Work: A Sandbox Is Reusable Only After It Forgets
item.description: Mastra’s public sandbox-pool patch treats reuse as a recovery problem: clean the worktree, separate credentials, and assume the machine may fail before it can be claimed again.

item.title: The Harness Was Taking the Test Too
item.description: OpenAI says two context choices lifted GPT-5.6 Sol from 13.3% to 38.3% on the ARC-AGI-3 public set. Codex source shows those “settings” are really a production memory system—and rival harnesses reveal how much of it can be copied.

item.title: An Agent Framework Can Carry Your Request—Not Your Responsibility
item.description: Microsoft Agent Framework's newest A2A and BYOK samples make one quiet operating rule visible: let a caller's configuration cross the boundary, but leave the host's policy and the provider's obligations where they belong.

item.title: Microsoft Agent Framework: the successor built from AutoGen and Semantic Kernel
item.description: Microsoft's new framework has migration paths for AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, but its freshest source work makes a more practical promise: carry a caller's intent across an agent boundary without letting it overrule the host that operates the run.

item.title: The Supervision Derby: four coding-agent control surfaces enter the first Diff Derby
item.description: The opening call gives Codex a narrow provisional edge for making subagent instruction precedence survive delegation and resume—but Qwen Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenHands each put a different kind of operator control on the track.

item.title: When an Agent Sees Two MCP Servers Called Docs
item.description: OpenClaw’s Code Mode has a new answer to a quietly consequential question: when several connected machines offer a server called docs , how does an agent know which one it is calling?

item.title: API Discovery: Tell an Agent When Waiting Is the Work
item.description: CrewAI’s new WaitTool gives an agent one narrow capability: let a real external job make progress before checking it again—without pretending that a pause is a status update.

item.title: PydanticAI: what type safety means when agents can act
item.description: A fresh cancellation fix draws the line clearly: typed inputs and validated outputs can discipline an agent’s interface, but a long-running run still needs a truthful answer to one operational question—did it actually stop?

item.title: Before Goose Runs a New Model, Pick Its Permission Mode
item.description: Goose has mapped Claude Opus 5 into its runtime. Before a new model reaches local tools, the operator still has to decide whether the session runs automatically, asks first, uses risk-based approval, or stays in chat.

item.title: Goose: one open agent runtime across models, tools, and local execution
item.description: A fresh Goose provider change adds Claude Opus 5 and adaptive-thinking support; the more consequential choice is still whether that model may act through local tools without asking first.
